ei.title: A Creative Idea Sparks a Whole New Field
ei.subject: 공통영어2

fullPassage: Criminals never leave a crime scene without leaving behind traces of their presence. The traces might be tiny, like hairs, or more obvious, such as soil from their shoes. So detectives carefully collect all the possible evidence. Scientists then analyze everything and find some clues. The clues are used to find the person who committed the crime. This process is called forensic science. It has evolved thanks to the contributions of many researchers. One of the most important people in the development of modern forensic science was Frances Glessner Lee. Frances Glessner Lee was born into a rich family in Chicago in 1878. She became interested in medicine at a young age. Her dream was to attend Harvard Medical School, but, at that time, the school did not accept women. She had no choice but to get married. It was not until she was in her fifties that Lee was able to start a career in medicine. Lee heard many interesting stories of real-life crime from her friend, George Burgess Magrath. He was a medical examiner who wanted to change the investigation system. This was because, at that time, people with no medical knowledge investigated and closed many death cases without examining the bodies. He also had a passion for educating medical students in legal medicine. Magrath’s passion sparked Lee’s interest in legal medicine. Lee started studying legal medicine by reading books and speaking with experts. She believed that medical examiner systems would be adopted more widely across the country. Furthermore, she wanted to see more young medical students trained in legal medicine. She decided to devote the rest of her life to developing this field. In 1931, she persuaded Harvard University to use her fortune to make a new branch of study: legal medicine. She also helped set up a library with rare books and documents. She thought laws had to be changed so that medical examiners had independent power. Public support was needed to change laws, so she used the World’s Fair held from 1939 to 1940 to educate the public about the modern medical examiner system. She also visited the governor with the chairman of the Department of Legal Medicine at Harvard. They talked about the importance of legal medicine. Thanks to Lee’s efforts, the Legal Medicine department at Harvard began to train future medical examiners in 1940. However, detectives were not careful with potential evidence. By touching and stepping on things, they often destroyed clues without realizing it. Due to this fact, analyzing the clues later was impossible. Lee thought detectives also had to learn how to observe crime scenes from a medical point of view. In order to educate detectives effectively, Lee came up with a creative tool. Her idea came from her hobby: creating miniatures. She started creating miniatures of crime scenes that were highly detailed and accurate. Based on real criminal cases, they included details like blood stains. Lee did not miss even the smallest detail, such as a small lamp or a label on a jar. She wanted to train detectives to notice tiny clues. She created around twenty miniature scenes during the 1940s and 1950s. In 1945, she held a week-long seminar and gave her first lecture using her miniature crime scenes. While reading case files, the detectives studied the details of the miniature scenes. They looked for clues in order to determine if the scene in the miniature resulted from an accident or a violent crime. The detectives learned to notice tiny details and to observe a scene without destroying any evidence. By developing their observation skills, they were able to improve their ability to solve crime cases. Lee’s training process was successful. By 1949, the annual seminar was being attended by detectives not only from the US but also from Canada. Special agents and military staff also attended the seminar. Lee died in 1962, after a career of more than thirty years. Although she had struggled to enter the field, her contributions to forensic science were significant. It is no wonder that she was called the “mother of forensic science.”

questions.passage: One of the most important people in the development of modern forensic science was Frances Glessner Lee.  Frances Glessner Lee was ①<u>born</u> into a rich family in Chicago in 1878.  She became ②<u>interesting</u> in medicine at a young age. questions.stem: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 ①~④ 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?

det.korean: ② interesting → interested: 사람이 '흥미를 느끼는' 것이므로 과거분사(-ed)
det.analysis:
❌ ① born — 'Lee was born into a rich family(Lee는 부유한 집안에서 태어났다)'예요. 'be born'은 '태어나다'라는 뜻으로 늘 이 형태를 쓰므로 올바릅니다.

✅ ② interesting — 원래는 interested입니다. 'She became interested in medicine(그녀는 의학에 흥미를 갖게 되었다)'처럼 사람이 '흥미를 느끼는' 상태는 과거분사 interested(-ed)로 써요. interesting(-ing)은 '(무엇이) 흥미로운'이라는 뜻이라 사람 주어와는 안 맞아요. ←정답

❌ ③ to attend — 'Her dream was to attend Harvard(그녀의 꿈은 하버드에 다니는 것이었다)'에서 'be동사 + to부정사(~하는 것)'로 올바릅니다.

❌ ④ to get — 'no choice but to get married(결혼하는 것 외에 선택의 여지가 없다)'에서 'but to부정사' 형태로 올바릅니다.
det.tip: -ing는 '남을 ~하게 하는', -ed는 '내가 ~한 감정을 느끼는' (사람=interested)

questions.stem: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 ①~④ 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?

det.korean: ③ examine → examining: 전치사 without 뒤에는 동명사(-ing)
det.analysis:
❌ ① able — 'Lee was able to start a career(Lee는 일을 시작할 수 있었다)'에서 'be able to(~할 수 있다)'로 올바릅니다.

❌ ② who wanted — 'a medical examiner who wanted to change(바꾸고 싶어 한 검시관)'에서 사람을 꾸며 주는 주격 관계대명사 who로 올바릅니다.

✅ ③ examine — 원래는 examining입니다. 앞의 without은 전치사인데, 전치사 뒤에는 동사를 그대로 못 쓰고 -ing(동명사)로 바꿔야 해요. 그래서 'without examining the bodies(시신을 검사하지 않고)'가 맞아요. examine(원형)은 틀려요. ←정답

❌ ④ educating — 'a passion for educating medical students(의대생을 가르치는 것에 대한 열정)'에서 전치사 for 뒤에 동명사 educating으로 올바릅니다.
det.tip: 전치사(without/for) + 동사 → 반드시 -ing(동명사)

Furthermore, she wanted to see more young medical students ②<u>trained</u> in legal medicine.  She decided to devote the rest of her life to ③<u>developing</u> this field. questions.stem: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 ①~④ 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?

det.korean: ① adopt → adopted: 'would be + 과거분사'로 '~되다'라는 수동태
det.analysis:
✅ ① adopt — 원래는 adopted입니다. 'systems would be ___(제도가 ~될 것이다)'는 제도가 '채택되는' 쪽(당하는 쪽)이라 수동태예요. 수동태는 'be동사 + 과거분사'이므로 'would be adopted(채택될 것이다)'가 맞아요. 원형 adopt는 틀려요. ←정답

❌ ② trained — 'see more students trained(더 많은 학생이 교육받는 것을 보다)'에서 'see + 목적어 + 과거분사'예요. 학생은 '교육을 받는' 대상이라 과거분사 trained가 올바릅니다.

❌ ③ developing — 'devote her life to developing this field(이 분야를 발전시키는 데 일생을 바치다)'에서 'devote A to -ing(~하는 데 A를 바치다)'의 to는 전치사라 뒤에 동명사가 와요. 올바릅니다.

❌ ④ to use — 'persuaded Harvard University to use her fortune(하버드가 재산을 쓰도록 설득했다)'에서 'persuade + 목적어 + to부정사'로 올바릅니다.
det.tip: would be adopted = 채택될 것이다 (제도는 '당하는' 쪽 → 수동태)

questions.passage: Criminals never leave a crime scene without leaving behind traces of their presence.  The traces might be ①<u>tiny</u>, like hairs, or more obvious, such as soil from their shoes.  So detectives carefully ②<u>collect</u> all the possible evidence.  Scientists then ③<u>analyze</u> everything and find some clues.  The clues are used to find the person who ④<u>prevented</u> the crime.  This process is called forensic science.
questions.stem: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 ①~④ 중, 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?

det.korean: ④ prevented → committed: 범죄를 '저지른' 사람을 찾는 것이므로 committed
det.analysis:
❌ ① tiny — 'The traces might be tiny, like hairs(흔적은 머리카락처럼 아주 작을 수 있다)'. 머리카락 예시와 어울리므로 '작은(tiny)'이 적절합니다.

❌ ② collect — 'detectives carefully collect all the possible evidence(형사들은 가능한 모든 증거를 조심스럽게 수집한다)'. 증거를 모은다는 문맥에 적절합니다.

❌ ③ analyze — 'Scientists then analyze everything(과학자들이 그다음 모든 것을 분석한다)'. 단서를 찾기 위해 분석한다는 문맥에 적절합니다.

✅ ④ prevented — 원래는 committed입니다. 단서는 '범죄를 저지른(committed)' 사람을 찾는 데 쓰여요. prevented(막았다)는 정반대라 문맥에 안 맞아요. ←정답
det.tip: commit a crime = 범죄를 저지르다 (↔ prevent 막다)

questions.passage: Thanks to Lee’s efforts, the Legal Medicine department at Harvard began to train future medical examiners in 1940.  However, detectives were not ①<u>careful</u> with potential evidence.  By touching and stepping on things, they often ②<u>preserved</u> clues without realizing it.  Due to this fact, analyzing the clues later was ③<u>impossible</u>.  Lee thought detectives also had to learn how to ④<u>observe</u> crime scenes from a medical point of view.  In order to educate detectives effectively, Lee came up with a creative tool.
questions.stem: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 ①~④ 중, 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?

det.korean: ② preserved → destroyed: 만지고 밟아서 단서를 '파괴한' 것이므로 destroyed
det.analysis:
❌ ① careful — 'detectives were not careful with potential evidence(형사들은 잠재적 증거에 조심하지 않았다)'. 뒤에 단서를 망친다는 내용이 이어지므로 '조심하는(careful)'이 적절합니다.

✅ ② preserved — 원래는 destroyed입니다. 앞에서 '만지고 밟음으로써(touching and stepping)'라고 했으니 단서를 '파괴했다(destroyed)'가 맞아요. preserved(보존했다)는 정반대라 틀려요. ←정답

❌ ③ impossible — 'analyzing the clues later was impossible(나중에 단서를 분석하는 것은 불가능했다)'. 단서를 망쳤으니 분석이 '불가능한(impossible)' 것이 적절합니다.

❌ ④ observe — 'learn how to observe crime scenes(범죄 현장을 관찰하는 법을 배우다)'. 현장을 살핀다는 문맥에 적절합니다.
det.tip: destroy clues = 단서를 파괴하다 (↔ preserve 보존하다)

questions.stem: 다음 글의 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

det.korean: 빈칸: 오십 대가 되어서야 '의학계에서 일을 시작할(start a career in medicine)' 수 있었다
det.analysis:
✅ ① start a career in medicine(의학계에서 일을 시작하다) — 어릴 때부터 의학에 관심이 있었지만 여자라서 하버드에 못 가고 결혼했다가, '오십 대가 되어서야(not until she was in her fifties)' 비로소 할 수 있었던 것은 '의학 관련 일을 시작하는 것'이에요. ←정답

❌ ② give up her lifelong dream(평생의 꿈을 포기하다) — 뒤에서 그녀가 법의학에 헌신하므로 꿈을 포기한 게 아니에요.

❌ ③ enter Harvard Medical School(하버드 의대에 입학하다) — 그 학교는 여성을 받지 않았다고 했으니 들어가지 못했어요.

❌ ④ open her own hospital(자신의 병원을 열다) — 본문에 병원을 열었다는 내용은 없어요.
det.tip: not until ~ = ~하고 나서야 비로소 (오십 대가 되어서야 시작)

questions.stem: 다음 글의 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

det.korean: 빈칸: 법을 바꾸려면 대중의 지지가 필요해서 '대중을 교육하기(educate the public)' 위해 세계 박람회를 이용했다
det.analysis:
❌ ① change the laws herself(직접 법을 바꾸다) — 빈칸 앞에서 '법을 바꾸려면 대중의 지지가 필요했다'고 했으니 혼자 바꾸는 게 아니에요.

❌ ② collect more of her fortune(재산을 더 모으다) — 돈을 더 모으는 내용이 아니에요.

✅ ③ educate the public(대중을 교육하다) — 'Public support was needed(대중의 지지가 필요했다)'가 근거예요. 그래서 세계 박람회를 이용해 '대중을 교육하려' 한 것이 자연스러워요. ←정답

❌ ④ train young detectives(젊은 형사들을 훈련하다) — 형사 훈련은 뒤에 나오는 다른 이야기이고, 여기서는 대중 대상이에요.
det.tip: Public support was needed → educate the public (대중 지지 얻기)

❌ ② Harvard Medical School은 Lee를 학생으로 받아들였다 — 본문은 'the school did not accept women(그 학교는 여성을 받지 않았다)'이라고 했어요.

❌ ③ Lee는 젊은 나이에 의사가 되어 일을 시작했다 — 본문은 'not until she was in her fifties(오십 대가 되어서야)' 일을 시작했다고 했어요.

questions.stem: 다음 글의 내용과 일치하지 않는 것은?

det.korean: ① 미국 형사들만 참석 — 캐나다 형사도 참석했으므로 불일치
det.analysis:
✅ ① 1949년에는 미국 형사들만 세미나에 참석했다 — 본문은 'detectives not only from the US but also from Canada(미국뿐 아니라 캐나다에서도)'라고 했어요. 미국만이 아니므로 일치하지 않아요. ←정답

❌ ② 형사들은 사건 파일을 읽으며 미니어처 장면의 세부 사항을 연구했다 — 'While reading case files, the detectives studied the details of the miniature scenes'와 일치해요.

questions.passage: Criminals never leave a crime scene without leaving behind traces of their presence.  The traces might be tiny, like hairs, or more obvious, such as soil from their shoes.  So detectives carefully collect all the possible evidence.  Scientists then analyze everything and find some clues.  The clues are used to find the person who committed the crime.  This process is called forensic science.  It has evolved thanks to the contributions of many researchers.  One of the most important people in the development of modern forensic science was Frances Glessner Lee.  Frances Glessner Lee was born into a rich family in Chicago in 1878.  She became interested in medicine at a young age.  Her dream was to attend Harvard Medical School, but, at that time, the school did not accept women.  She had no choice but to get married.  It was not until she was in her fifties that Lee was able to start a career in medicine.  Lee heard many interesting stories of real-life crime from her friend, George Burgess Magrath.  He was a medical examiner who wanted to change the investigation system.  This was because, at that time, people with no medical knowledge investigated and closed many death cases without examining the bodies.  He also had a passion for educating medical students in legal medicine.  Magrath’s passion sparked Lee’s interest in legal medicine.  Lee started studying legal medicine by reading books and speaking with experts.  She believed that medical examiner systems would be adopted more widely across the country.  Furthermore, she wanted to see more young medical students trained in legal medicine.  She decided to devote the rest of her life to developing this field.  In 1931, she persuaded Harvard University to use her fortune to make a new branch of study: legal medicine.  She also helped set up a library with rare books and documents.  She thought laws had to be changed so that medical examiners had independent power.  Public support was needed to change laws, so she used the World’s Fair held from 1939 to 1940 to educate the public about the modern medical examiner system.  She also visited the governor with the chairman of the Department of Legal Medicine at Harvard.  They talked about the importance of legal medicine.  Thanks to Lee’s efforts, the Legal Medicine department at Harvard began to train future medical examiners in 1940.  However, detectives were not careful with potential evidence.  By touching and stepping on things, they often destroyed clues without realizing it.  Due to this fact, analyzing the clues later was impossible.  Lee thought detectives also had to learn how to observe crime scenes from a medical point of view.  In order to educate detectives effectively, Lee came up with a creative tool.  Her idea came from her hobby: creating miniatures.  She started creating miniatures of crime scenes that were highly detailed and accurate.  Based on real criminal cases, they included details like blood stains.  Lee did not miss even the smallest detail, such as a small lamp or a label on a jar.  She wanted to train detectives to notice tiny clues.  She created around twenty miniature scenes during the 1940s and 1950s.  In 1945, she held a week-long seminar and gave her first lecture using her miniature crime scenes.  While reading case files, the detectives studied the details of the miniature scenes.  They looked for clues in order to determine if the scene in the miniature resulted from an accident or a violent crime.  The detectives learned to notice tiny details and to observe a scene without destroying any evidence.  By developing their observation skills, they were able to improve their ability to solve crime cases.  Lee’s training process was successful.  By 1949, the annual seminar was being attended by detectives not only from the US but also from Canada.  Special agents and military staff also attended the seminar.  Lee died in 1962, after a career of more than thirty years.  Although she had struggled to enter the field, her contributions to forensic science were significant.  It is no wonder that she was called the “mother of forensic science.

det.analysis:
'~하는 것 외에 선택의 여지가 없다'라는 표현을 배열하는 문제예요.

① '그녀는 선택의 여지가 없었다'는 she had no choice예요. 'have no choice'가 '선택의 여지가 없다'는 뜻이에요.

② '~하는 것 외에는'은 'but to + 동사원형'으로 나타내요. 'no choice but to(~하는 것 외에 선택의 여지가 없다)'는 통째로 외워두면 좋은 표현이에요.

③ '결혼하다'는 get married예요. 그래서 but to get married가 돼요.

전부 이으면 she had no choice but to get married, 총 8단어예요.
det.tip: have no choice but to + 동사원형 = ~하는 수밖에 없다

questions.wa: she had no choice but to get married
accept: she had no choice but to get married
